chunks: Test stations on an assembly line. The question: What are a few test stations you would see on an electronics manufacturing/assembly line?
An assembly line has a series of stations, and each one answers a different question about the board. Some look at the solder paste or the finished soldering.
Some check the electrical connections. One loads firmware. One runs the board like the real product. Failed boards go to a repair bench.
All stations log results under the board's serial number.
Think of a car wash with several stops: rinse, soap, brush, rinse, dry. Each stop does one job, and cars move through on a conveyor.
The whole wash can only go as fast as its slowest stop, so a slow brush stage makes a queue behind it. A board line works the same way.
The slowest station sets the pace for every board, no matter how fast the others are.
A representative layout.
Boards flow left to right through printing and inspection, electrical test, programming and functional test, then through any safety or RF station to final QA.
Failures peel off (red dashed) to the repair bench and re-enter the flow.
Inspection stations: cameras and scanners that look at paste, parts and joints, such as AOI. In-circuit test: a fixture of probes that checks shorts, opens and part values.
Flying probe: a few moving probes that do a similar check with no custom fixture.
Programming station: loads firmware (the program stored in the board's chip) and the serial number. Functional test station: powers and exercises the board.
Say AOI takes 30 seconds per board, in-circuit test 40 seconds, programming 60 seconds and functional test 45 seconds.
Programming is the slowest, so the line makes 3600 / 60 = 60 boards per hour. Add a second programming station, so it effectively takes 30 seconds per board.
Now functional test at 45 seconds is the slowest, and the line makes 3600 / 45 = 80 boards per hour. That is the whole idea.
"After reflow I'd expect AOI with cameras checking part presence and solder, X-ray for BGAs, then an electrical test station: in-circuit test with a bed-of-nails fixture, or a flying probe machine.
Then a programming station for firmware and serial numbers and a functional test station that powers and exercises the board.
Depending on the product there's also RF calibration, hipot, and a burn-in chamber, with final inspection and a repair bench. Everything logs to a database by serial number."
